# Estimating the impact of state paid sick leave laws on worker outcomes in the U.S. service sector, 2017–2023☆

**Authors:** Tyler Woods; Daniel Schneider; Kristen Harknett

**Affiliations:** aHarvard Kennedy School, United States | bUniversity of California, San Francisco, United States

## Abstract

In the absence of a federal paid sick leave (PSL) standard, numerous U.S. states have passed laws to provide workers access to such benefits. These laws may be especially beneficial for low-wage workers whose employers often do not voluntarily provide PSL. We draw on novel data from The Shift Project (N = 68,930), which surveyed U.S. service sector workers between 2017 and 2023, to examine the effects of state PSL laws on proximate worker outcomes (i.e., PSL coverage and presenteeism), downstream worker outcomes (e.g., health, well-being, and labor market outcomes), and firms' channels of adjustment (e.g., hourly wages, work schedules, other fringe benefits). We use stacked difference-in-differences models to estimate the effects of 11 state PSL laws on service sector workers, leveraging the time horizon and scope of our data to make comparisons between treatment and control states before and after the implementation of such laws. We find that state PSL laws increased hourly service sector workers’ access to PSL by 14 percentage points (p < 0.001) and reduced the share of workers who worked while sick by 3 percentage points (p < 0.01). In addition, we find little evidence that firms offset the costs of providing PSL by reducing other benefits for workers. This increase in PSL coverage among service sector workers and their reduced likelihood of working while sick could have significant positive implications for public health. But, we also show that PSL laws have little demonstrable effect on other downstream health, well-being, and labor market outcomes for covered workers.

## Abstract

•State PSL laws increase service sector workers' PSL access and reduce presenteeism.•Firms did not offset PSL costs by reducing wages, benefits, or schedule stability.•PSL laws have few effects on downstream health, well-being, and labor market outcomes.

## Introduction

The U.S. is one of few developed nations that has no federally mandated paid sick leave (PSL) (Heymann et al., 2009). Many states, counties, and cities have passed PSL laws to fill this gap, while other locales have preemptively banned PSL mandates, resulting in patchwork coverage across the country (Pomeranz et al., 2022). Even the passage of PSL mandates does not guarantee coverage, as there is extensive non-compliance among employers with labor laws (Armenia et al., 2014), evidenced by widespread wage and hour violations (Galvin, 2016; Schneider et al., 2024).

Prior research has considered the effect of PSL laws on a host of outcomes, including proximate worker outcomes (e.g., PSL coverage and presenteeism) and downstream outcomes (e.g., well-being and labor market outcomes). To date, though, findings on the impact of PSL laws on these worker outcomes are mixed or suffer from methodological limitations. For example, there is some evidence that PSL mandates are effective at increasing PSL coverage and reducing the extent to which workers attend work while sick (Callison & Pesko, 2022; Colla et al., 2014; Maclean et al., 2020; Romich, 2017; Schneider, 2020), although this work is often either associational or uses methods that have more recently been shown to be unsuitable for complex policy interventions (e.g., staggered adoption periods). Opponents of PSL mandates often argue that such mandates impose costs on employers that might be offset through worker-facing channels of adjustment such as wages, other benefits, or schedules (Gruber, 1994; Summers, 1989). But, relatively little prior scholarship has investigated whether firms offset the costs associated with providing PSL by reducing other elements of workers' job quality, such as wages, work schedule stability, or other non-mandated benefits. Existing research is mixed, as some evidence suggests little demonstrable effects on wages (Pichler & Ziebarth, 2020) while others find positive spillover effects for non-mandated benefits like health insurance (Maclean et al., 2020), but little work has examined a broad set of such channels of adjustment. Finally, the extant literature makes broad claims about the impact of PSL laws on more distal worker outcomes, including psychological distress, self-reported health, economic security, job stability, and healthcare utilization (Hill, 2013; Jeung et al., 2021; Lamsal et al., 2021; Slopen, 2023, 2024; Stoddard-Dare et al., 2018), though other work finds few effects on workers’ labor market outcomes (Wething, 2021) or experiences of work-life conflict (Schneider, 2020). However, this work is often associational and rarely uses advanced causal inference methods (but see Slopen, 2023, 2024).

In this paper, we address several limitations in the scholarship on the effects of PSL mandates on worker outcomes. First, research on the effects of PSL mandates on PSL coverage often relies on employer reports of PSL provision (Colla et al., 2014; Maclean et al., 2020; Romich, 2017), which may not align with workers' actual on-the-job experiences of PSL access. We draw on direct worker reports rather than employer reports of PSL provision. Second, much of this work is associational rather than relying on causal inference methods (e.g., Harknett & Schneider, 2022), and the existing studies that do use causal frameworks are often limited in timeframe (i.e., only examining short-run effects) or scope (i.e., only focusing on a small number of locales). Furthermore, these studies typically rely on two-way fixed effects and standard difference-in-differences models to derive causal estimates (Callison & Pesko, 2022; Schneider, 2020), but recent advances in causal identification highlight biases in these methods when studying policies with staggered adoption timelines and multiple time periods (Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021; Wing, Freedman, and Hollingsworth, 2024). We propose a robust causal identification strategy that examines more states over a longer timeframe. Third, many studies examine a small number of outcomes, meaning that the comparability of findings across studies is low, as few papers have examined a wide range of outcomes on the same sample. In this paper, we examine a holistic set of worker outcomes on the same sample using up-to-date methods for causal inference.

Finally, access to employer-provided PSL is stratified by socioeconomic status. Despite disparities in PSL access (Gupta et al., 2018), prior research often combines workers across job types when examining the effects of PSL (though, see Callison and Pesko (2022) and Maclean et al. (2020)). But, the role of PSL mandates is of particular relevance in some subsectors, including the service sector. Indeed, service sector jobs are lower quality to begin with across various metrics (Schneider and Harknett, 2019) and have among the lowest rates of PSL access (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024). Further, the need for PSL is potentially even greater for service sector workers, as these jobs inherently involve higher risk of exposure to infectious disease, given the density and traffic of indoor workplace settings (Wolfe, Harknett, and Schneider, 2021; Woods, Schneider, and Harknett, 2023).

We leverage a unique data source to explore the effects of PSL laws on hourly service sector workers in the U.S. Drawing on data from The Shift Project (N = 68,930), we examine how state PSL mandates affect worker outcomes, including proximate outcomes such as access to PSL and presenteeism; downstream health, well-being, and employment outcomes; and channels of adjustment that firms may use to offset the increased cost of providing PSL.

## Backround

### Paid sick leave in the U.S

Paid sick leave (PSL) affords workers’ the ability to take paid leave from their job to recover from illness, access health care, or help to care for an ill family member. Unlike most industrialized nations, the U.S. does not mandate PSL at the federal level; rather, the decision to offer PSL benefits is left to the discretion of individual employers (Pomeranz et al., 2022). As a result, employee access to PSL is highly unequal, as often only “good” employers offer these benefits (Slopen, 2023). This inequality is particularly stark among low-wage workers in the service sector (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024; Callison & Pesko, 2022; Gupta et al., 2018).

In order to ensure some minimum level of paid sick leave for workers, many states, counties, and cities have passed their own legislation to mandate PSL provision by employers (Pomeranz et al., 2022). While there are broad similarities between policies (Mitchell, 2024), there is also some variation in the comprehensiveness of these PSL laws, including their generosity, their inclusion criteria for employees and firms, and in the autonomy with which workers are able to use their PSL benefits (Wething, 2022). For example, policies differ in the minimum number of employees for employers to be covered by the policy, the amount of leave provided, and the covered reasons for using leave (Mitchell, 2024; Wething, 2022). However, at their core, these policies all offer workers the ability to take paid leave when sick, and the staggered implementation across states over time presents a unique opportunity to test the impacts of these policies on workers.

### PSL mandates and PSL access and presenteeism

There is a large literature across sociology and public health on the effects of PSL laws on a host of worker outcomes, both proximate and distal. Many of these studies focus on the most direct outcome: employees' access to PSL. While prior research has estimated the effect of PSL laws on PSL coverage, much of this research relies on employer reports (Colla et al., 2014; Romich, 2017), which may be biased given employers’ incentive to report compliance with labor standards against a backdrop of widespread violations (Schneider et al., 2024). Studies using employer reports find that the provision of PSL increases significantly following PSL legislation, though they are often conducted over a short time period and in a single location (e.g., Seattle or San Francisco) (Colla et al., 2014; Romich, 2017).

The limited studies using worker reports suggest that PSL laws significantly increase the provision of PSL (Callison & Pesko, 2022; Schneider, 2020). For example, Schneider (2020) finds that service sector workers in Washington saw a 28 percentage point increase in PSL access following the implementation of the PSL mandate. Recent studies using national samples also find that PSL laws increase coverage most among workers who likely lacked PSL prior to the mandate (Callison & Pesko, 2022; Maclean et al., 2020).

However, many of these studies rely on standard difference-in-differences models, which may introduce bias because of treatment effect heterogeneity (Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021; Wing et al., 2024), though Maclean et al.’s (2020) recent study is an exception. Drawing on data from the National Compensation Survey (which relies on employer reports of PSL provision, rather than worker-side reports), Maclean and colleagues (2020) show that PSL coverage increased by 30 percentage points and had the greatest “bite” in industries with low levels of pre-mandate coverage, such as food service.

In addition to these effects on PSL access, PSL mandates may also affect presenteeism in the workplace (i.e., working while sick). Presenteeism is a widespread problem in the U.S (Susser & Ziebarth, 2016) and has notable public health implications (Widera, Chang, and Chen, 2010), as workers who attend work while sick are more likely to spread illness to coworkers and, in customer-facing occupations like retail and food service, to customers (Moritz et al., 2023). When workers lack PSL, they are more likely to work while sick (DeRigne et al., 2016), and this is likely particularly true among low-wage hourly workers, for whom staying home while sick without paid leave means forgoing vital income. Conversely, as workers gain access to PSL through mandates at the state and local levels, they experience reductions in working while sick (Callison & Pesko, 2022; Schneider, 2020). Little research, though, uses advanced causal inference methods to estimate the effect of PSL mandates on presenteeism, instead relying on associational regression models (e.g., DeRigne et al., 2016) or standard difference-in-difference models (e.g., Schneider, 2020), which may produce biased estimates in contexts with staggered adoption and multiple time periods (Wing et al., 2024).

### Channels of adjustment for PSL

Expansions of 10.13039/501100009517PSL benefits impose a mandate on employers but do not provide a public funding mechanism for any associated costs. Employers may compensate for the added costs of mandatory benefits provision by reducing labor costs through wage, benefit, or scheduling-related adjustments (Gruber, 1994; Summers, 1989). Prior research has shown that employers rely on a number of such “channels of adjustment” to absorb the costs associated with minimum wage increases, including higher prices, lower profit margins, and wage compression, though there are few discernible impacts on employment outcomes (Bodnár et al., 2018; Hirsch, Kaufman, and Zelenska, 2015; Schmitt, 2000). A small body of research has explored whether a similar process unfolds for PSL mandates.

When mandated to provide PSL to their employees, some firms may decide to cut wages, more carefully manage scheduled hours, or reduce other ancillary benefits (e.g., health insurance) to offset the added costs of PSL. The existing empirical evidence on employers' channels of adjustment for PSL is mixed, as some research shows that there are no discernible wages effects (Pichler & Ziebarth, 2020), while other work has found that there may be positive spillover effects of providing PSL to other non-mandated fringe benefits (Maclean et al., 2020). For example, Maclean and colleagues (2020) document evidence of “job upscaling”: PSL mandates increase the likelihood that firms will offer other fringe benefits, such as health, prescription drug, and disability insurance. The authors hypothesize that this “crowding in” might stem from employers wanting to signal higher job quality to recruit workers. In contrast, Pichler and Ziebarth (2020) find little evidence that PSL mandates affect workers’ wages, although they do find small but non-significant wage decreases.

However, prior research on channels of adjustment for PSL rarely provide estimates at the individual level, as Pichler and Ziebarth (2020) use county-level data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) to assess aggregate employment and wage effects, while Maclean et al. (2020) draw on firm-job level data from the National Compensation Survey (NCS) to assess job-level effects. While individual-level data that relies on employee self-reports may suffer from some amount of recall bias, it also allows for a greater level of analytical specificity and a more extensive set of controls for potential confounders. Furthermore, little research examines a broad set of potential channels of adjustment simultaneously, and no research to date considers the potential impact of PSL mandates on work schedule instability, a highly consequential element of job quality for low-wage workers in the service sector.

### Distal effects of PSL on worker outcomes

The extant literature on PSL access makes broad claims concerning the effects of workers' access to PSL on more distal downstream outcomes, such as workers’ health, well-being, and labor market outcomes. As Slopen (2023) notes, access to PSL may help workers access health care and reduce the stress associated with either taking unpaid time off or attending work while sick, with positive implications for worker health and well-being. Scholars have also hypothesized that the provision of PSL may improve job stability and reduce turnover, to the extent that it constitutes an improvement in job quality that allows workers to deal with health needs without risking separation (Hill, 2013; Wething, 2021), although others suggest that there may be negative effects on employment outcomes if workers are willing to accept lower paying jobs to access PSL (Hill, 2013; Slopen, 2024). However, the evidence on these downstream outcomes is mixed and often relies on either associational or outdated causal inference methods. Furthermore, often due to data limitations, these studies rarely consider a broad set of health, well-being, and labor market outcomes simultaneously, making it difficult to determine whether the mixed findings stem from differences in sample composition and model specification or from true empirical differences.

Scholarship tends to show that PSL mandates have positive effects on workers' health and well-being. For example, studies that rely primarily on associational methods find that workers' access to PSL is associated with improvements in psychological distress (Stoddard-Dare et al., 2018) and increased healthcare use, such as seeing a doctor or receiving a flu vaccine (Lamsal et al., 2021). Research that draws on standard difference-in-difference models, which are unable to account for dynamic treatment effects in policy contexts with staggered adoption, similarly finds that PSL mandates are associated with increased use of preventative services (Jeung et al., 2021), although Schneider (2020) finds little evidence that PSL mandates affect workers’ experiences of work-life conflict. Additionally, Pichler et al. (2021) find evidence of positive health externalities of mandating PSL, specifically reduced rates of influenza-like illness (ILI) at the population level. Finally, some recent work utilizes advanced causal inference methods that address potential bias due to heterogenous treatment effects to show that PSL mandates are associated with improvements in health, specifically for women (Slopen, 2023), as well as mental health treatment (Maclean et al., 2020).

Research on the labor market effects of PSL is limited and the findings are more mixed. For example, Hill (2013) uses associational regression models to show that workers who have access to PSL are less likely to experience job separation, while Wething (2021) uses standard difference-in-difference models to document no substantive effects of PSL mandates on hires, separations, or turnover. Additionally, some studies that use advanced causal inference methods find that PSL laws increase women's employment and economic security (Slopen, 2024), while others find no discernible effect on employment outcomes (Pichler & Ziebarth, 2020).

## Methods

### Data

We draw on pooled cross-sectional data on a national sample of workers at large firms in the service sector, which includes food service, retail, hospitality, general merchandise, and grocery. These data come from The Shift Project, which leverages Facebook users' employer information to sample and recruit workers at large service sector firms using targeted advertisements (Schneider and Harknett, 2022). These advertisements appear in users' feeds on Facebook and Instagram, offering a lottery incentive for participation in the study. Upon clicking the advertisement, users are directed to the Qualtrics survey platform, where they provide consent to participate and complete a brief (20-min) online survey. These questions cover a broad range of topics, including workers’ job quality (e.g., wages, work schedules, benefits), benefits receipt, health and well-being, and demographic characteristics. Since 2016, The Shift Project has collected 16 waves of cross-sectional data through twice-annual data collection, including data on almost 200,000 workers at over 200 firms. We also compile a database that documents state and local policies that affect labor conditions (e.g., minimum wage, PSL), which allows us to track the implementation of PSL mandates across place and over time (by month), as well as to control for other potentially confounding policy interventions (e.g., minimum wage laws).

To ensure comparability across survey waves, we limit our sample to waves that span the period Fall 2017 through Fall 2023. Eleven states implemented PSL laws during this period: Colorado, Connecticut, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, and Washington. We exclude states that passed PSL mandates prior to the beginning of our data collection (Arizona, California, District of Columbia, Massachusetts, Oregon, and Vermont), as we have no pre-treatment data for these locales and are unable to estimate the effect of treatment. We also exclude sub-state locales that passed PSL mandates because our sample sizes at the county level are too small to sufficiently power these analyses. Therefore, we restrict our sample to workers within 11 states that passed PSL during the study period and 34 control states that had not passed PSL as of Fall 2023. Our final sample includes 68,930 workers at 204 service sector firms with complete information on all covariates. While these data are not nationally representative and rely on a non-probability sampling approach, they have been benchmarked against “gold standard” probability samples (e.g. CPS, NLSY) and are robust to a number of data validity checks that reduce concerns around selection based on both observable and unobservable characteristics (Schneider and Harknett, 2022). Furthermore, recent reports suggest a vast majority (68 %) of U.S. adults are active on Facebook and nearly half (47 %) are active on Instagram (Gottfried, 2024), reducing concerns around non-coverage.

### Key variables

#### Treatment

We compile a database of PSL policies across all U.S. states and counties from 2013 to 2023 using publicly available information (e.g., state or county legal code, third-party policy trackers). We then create a monthly measure of PSL laws that codes state-month periods as “0” if there is no policy in effect and “1” if there is a policy in effect. We merge this information into the Shift Project micro-data by respondents’ state of employment and survey month. To accurately capture where workers are employed, respondents are asked to report precise establishment location and are then matched to geocoded store information that we scrape from publicly available data online. For those who do not directly report store location, we rely on the self-reported state of work and, when missing, on geocoded Internet Protocol (IP) addresses captured through the Qualtrics survey platform. This gives us a treatment measure (presence of state PSL mandate) that varies by place and time.

#### Proximate outcomes

We examine two proximate outcomes of PSL mandates: PSL coverage and presenteeism. To capture PSL coverage, we draw on a measure that asks workers what benefits their employers offer: “Please look at the following list of benefits that employers sometimes make available to their employees. Which of the benefits on this list can you receive as part of your job at [EMPLOYER NAME]? Please mark all that apply.” One option was “paid sick days.” To capture presenteeism, we draw on a measure that asks if respondents worked in the past month while sick: “In the past month, did you ever work at [EMPLOYER NAME] even though you were feeling sick?” The response options included “Yes”, “No, I was sick but stayed home”, and “No, I haven't been sick in the past month.” We then create a dichotomous measure comparing workers who were sick in the past month (“Did not work while sick” vs. “Worked while sick”).

#### Channels of adjustment

To examine whether employers absorb the costs of implementing PSL in ways that affect workers, we test four potential channels of adjustment: hourly wage, schedule instability, health insurance benefits, and retirement benefits. We use a measure of workers' hourly wage without tips. Our measures of health insurance and retirement benefits come from the same question as paid sick leave benefits, which asks workers to report which benefits are offered by their employer. “Health plan or medical insurance” and “A retirement plan other than social security” were both response options. We use a five-point scale of schedule instability that measures workers’ exposure to five unstable scheduling practices in the past month: canceled shifts, changed shift timing, on-call shifts, clopening shifts (i.e., working an opening shift immediately after working a closing shift the previous night), and less than two weeks of advanced notice. Schedule instability is one potential channel of adjustment not only for the cost savings associated with just-in-time scheduling, but also because firms may be more likely to make last minute schedule changes if workers call out sick more because of PSL benefits.

#### Downstream outcomes

We test the effect of PSL mandates on several “downstream” health, well-being, and labor market outcomes, including self-rated health, psychological distress, happiness, sleep quality, job satisfaction, turnover intentions, and work-life conflict. We draw on a measure of self-rated health that asks respondents “In general, how is your health? Would you say it is …” with response options that included “Excellent,” “Very good,” “Good,” “Fair”, and “Poor.” To capture psychological distress, we draw on the Kessler-6 index, which asks respondents how often in that past month they felt 1) so sad nothing could cheer them up; 2) nervous; 3) restless; 4) hopeless; 5) worthless; and 6) like everything was an effort. The response options ranged from “None of the time” (0) to “All of the time” (4). We summed these into an index (0–24) and then dichotomized the index to high psychological distress (12 or above) or low psychological distress, in line with prior work (Prochaska et al., 2012). We also use a measure of sleep quality, which asks respondents “During the past month, how would you rate your sleep quality overall?” Response options included “Very good,” “Good”, “Fair”, and “Poor.” We dichotomize this measure to high sleep quality (very good or good sleep) and low sleep quality (fair or poor sleep). Finally, we include a measure of happiness, which asks respondents “Taken all together, how would you say things are these days? Would you say you are …”, with response options that included “Very happy,” “Pretty happy,” and “Not too happy.” We dichotomize this to be happy (very or pretty happy) and not happy (not too happy).

We next include a measure of job satisfaction, which asks respondents “All in all, how satisfied would you say you are with your job at [EMPLOYER NAME]?”, with options including “Very satisfied”, “Somewhat satisfied”, “Not too satisfied", and “Not at all satisfied.” To gauge respondents' intentions to leave their jobs, we ask “Taking everything into consideration, how likely is it you will make a genuine effort to find a new job within the next 3 months?” Response options include “Very likely,” “Somewhat likely”, and “Not at all likely.” Finally, we capture respondents’ experiences of work-like conflict using a scale consisting of three items: 1) “In my work schedule at [EMPLOYER NAME], I have enough flexibility to handle family needs; 2) “At [EMPLOYER NAME], it is difficult to deal with family or personal matters during working hours.”; and 3) “Do you agree or disagree? It is easy to get time off from [EMPLOYER NAME] when I need it.” Response options for the first two items included “Always true”, “Often true”, “Sometimes true”, and “Never true”, while the options for the last item included “Strongly agree”, “Agree”, “Disagree”, and “Strongly disagree.” We standardized the direction and summed these items to create a work-life conflict scale (3–12).

#### Control variables

We account for potentially confounding variables in our analysis, including demographic characteristics (gender, age, race/ethnicity, marital status, parental status, school enrollment, English as a Second Language), work characteristics (job tenure, union membership, managerial status), and a time-varying measure of state minimum wage. We summarize the composition of the treated and control samples in Table 1. They are very closely matched, with the exception of union status, which is higher in treatment locations. Union status, like the other characteristics in the table, is controlled in the models.

### Analysis

We employ a stacked difference-in-differences design to estimate the effect of state PSL laws on worker outcomes. Difference-in-differences models are typically constrained to two time periods (before and after policy intervention) and two groups (those treated with the intervention and a control group), but these models must be modified for complicated policy contexts that include multiple time periods or when units are exposed to treatment at different times (i.e., staggered adoption) (Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021; Wing et al., 2024). Social scientists have frequently relied on two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression models to estimate causal effects in these scenarios. However, recent methodological advances have pointed to issues with the TWFE design, namely that TWFE estimates group early and late adopters together, which, in the presence of heterogeneous time effects, could violate the parallel trends assumption (Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021; Wing et al., 2024).

Scholars have recently proposed several solutions to analyzing the causal effects of policy interventions that are adopted at different times by different units, including the Callaway and Sant’Anna difference-in-difference estimator (Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021) and the stacked difference-in-differences model (Wing et al., 2024). The former has been used in several recently published papers on the effects of state PSL laws (e.g., Maclean et al., 2020; Slopen, 2023, 2024). In this paper, we draw upon the latter, which builds upon the Callaway and Sant’Anna approach by ensuring compositional balance between pre- and post-treatment units and calculating an aggregate parameter in a linear regression framework that is highly interpretable. The stacked difference-in-differences approach involves constructing separate data sets for each “sub-experiment,” which consist of one treated location and all valid controls for that location, then vertically combining these sub-experimental datasets into a stacked analytic file (Wing et al., 2024). In this data structure, respondents in early- and late-adopting states are not compared against each other, but rather only with respondents in clean control states, addressing concerns about potential treatment effect heterogeneity. We compute an average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) parameter in this stacked regression framework, with standard errors clustered at the state level (i.e., the treatment unit). We created event study graphs (Appendix Figs. 1–3) for each outcome, which show that the parallel trends assumption holds for all models.

Additionally, we adjust the stacked difference-in-differences approach proposed by Wing and colleagues (Wing et al., 2024) to fit our research design. While the authors use observations at the treated-unit level, we use individual-level data where respondents are nested within treated or untreated states. Second, because our pre-treatment period is on average about one year shorter than our post-treatment period, we make alterations to the trimmed aggregate ATT weight proposed by Wing et al., creating separate aggregate ATT weights for pre- and post-treatment observations. In Appendix Table 1, we trim our sample for compositional balance, drawing on five states with four waves of pre-treatment data and six waves of post-treatment data, and our results are fully robust to this specification. We do not use this as our primary model to leverage all treated states. We do trim our sample to only include respondents in relative time periods with at least 2 treatment states and at least 500 respondents to ensure the models are sufficiently powered. Third, following other work using stacked difference-in-differences models (Butters et al., 2022; Cengiz et al., 2019), we also include state-by-sub-experiment and time-by-sub-experiment fixed effects in our models, measuring time as survey wave. Because our study period includes the COVID-19 pandemic, which significantly affected health and labor market outcomes, our time-based fixed effects also function to net out these effects.

We estimate linear probability models for binary outcomes and OLS regression models for continuous outcomes. We begin with a simple model regressing each outcome (Y) on the PSL treatment variable (T) interacted with a binary measure of pre-/post-implementation (P) (equation (1)), then add vectors of sociodemographic (D) and work (W) controls and a time-varying control for state minimum wage (M) (equation (2)), and then year-by-sub-experiment ( γ y ) and state-by-sub-experiment ( δ s ) fixed effects (equation (3)). ## Results

### Proximate outcomes

In Table 2, we present the results for models estimating the effect of state PSL laws on two proximate outcomes: PSL coverage and presenteeism. Considering the fully adjusted model (M3 of Table 2), service sector workers experienced a 14 percentage point increase in access to PSL at work following implementation of a state PSL law relative to the control group (b = 0.139, p < 0.001). Taking predicted probabilities, we see that respondents in treatment states saw a gain in PSL coverage of 16 percentage points (from 46 % to 62 %), while respondents in control states saw a gain of only 2 percentage points (from 37 % to 39 %). ### Channels of adjustment

We next estimate the effect of state PSL laws on channels of adjustments within firms, particularly those that have direct implications for workers: hourly wages, schedule instability, health insurance benefits, and retirement benefits. Table 3 presents the results from these models. Relative to those in control states, workers in treatment states saw no reduction in wages, no decreases in health insurance or retirement benefits, and no increases in schedule instability. These findings align with Pichler and Ziebarth (2020) insofar as we find no negative effects of PSL on workers’ wages, a positive sign that employers do not reduce wages as a channel of adjustment following PSL implementation, although Pichler and Ziebarth find small but non-significant wage decreases while we find small but non-significant wage increases. In contrast to Maclean and colleagues (2020), we also find little evidence of “crowding in,” or rather the positive spillover effects of PSL into other non-mandated benefits. ### Downstream outcomes

Finally, in Fig. 2, we plot coefficients from regression models estimating the effect of state PSL laws on myriad downstream outcomes. Across this broad set of measures, we show that PSL mandates have little demonstrable effect on more distal outcomes. Most are in the expected direction but are not statistically significant, although the coefficient for job satisfaction is in the opposite direction that what we would expect (albeit with a tiny effect size). Thus, while the literature has made broad claims around the potential for PSL legislation to have positive effects on myriad health, well-being, and labor market outcomes, we find limited evidence of this in our analysis. ### Robustness checks

In supplementary analyses, we conduct a number of checks to determine the robustness of our results to alternative specifications. First, as described above, we trim our sample to achieve compositional balance and find that our results are fully robust to this trimmed and balanced sample (Appendix Table 1). Second, we use test the robustness of our results to alternative weighting schemes, including weighting our analysis equally across the 11 sub-experiments and weighting based on the population of the treated states. We find similar results for our primary outcomes (Appendix Tables 2 and 3), although the effect of PSL mandates on presenteeism is only marginally significant using equal weights. Finally, to establish a reference point to prior work, we also run two-way fixed effects models and document similar results (Appendix Table 4), suggesting there may be little treatment effect heterogeneity for PSL mandates across states and over time.

## Discussion

Given the lack of federal paid sick leave (PSL) in the U.S., state mandates are one lever to increase PSL coverage among low-wage workers, with the potential to have downstream positive effects for workers and for public health. However, much of the existing scholarship on PSL coverage relies on employer reports, and those studies that do use worker reports rarely use advanced causal inference methods and are often limited in timeframe or in scope (Callison & Pesko, 2022; DeRigne et al., 2016). Furthermore, little research has leveraged these novel causal inference methods (e.g., Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021; Wing et al., 2024) to estimate the effects of state PSL laws on employee-facing channels of adjustment (e.g., wages) or on downstream health, well-being, and labor market outcomes. Finally, scholars rarely consider these outcomes simultaneously, meaning that the differing effects of PSL on proximate and downstream outcomes across studies could be driven by differences in sample composition and model specification rather than meaningful empirical relationships.

We address these gaps by drawing on data from The Shift Project to identify the causal effects of state PSL laws on outcomes for a group of workers of prime policy interest. Using stacked difference-in-differences models, we show that state PSL laws increase the share of workers who have access to PSL at work by 14 percentage points and decrease the share of workers who work while sick by 3 percentage points. This finding is in line with previous work on the topic (Callison & Pesko, 2022; Schneider, 2020), but our estimates are novel insofar as they are focused on a subset of the worker population at heightened need for PSL and cover more time and more states than many previous studies. We find no evidence that the adoption of PSL within firms comes at the expense of other elements of job quality, such as wages, schedules, or other fringe benefits, in contrast to work that found PSL laws lead to “crowding in” by increasing firms' provision of other fringe benefits (Maclean et al., 2020). Our study is novel in its inclusion of work schedule instability as a potential channel of adjustment. However, in contrast to prior studies that find positive effects of PSL laws on workers’ health and well-being, including psychological distress (Stoddard-Dare et al., 2018) and self-rated health (Slopen, 2023), we show that PSL laws have little impact on these outcomes, although our estimates are in the expected direction but not statistically significant. The preponderance of evidence, therefore, is that the downstream positive benefits of PSL laws are likely quite modest in size. Other research has posited that downstream effects could emerge with a longer follow-up period (Schneider, 2020), but we find no demonstrable effects even with a longer time horizon of over three years.

There are several potential explanations for why we find relatively modest effects of PSL mandates on presenteeism and null effects on downstream outcomes. First, the COVID-19 pandemic significantly altered social norms on working while sick, increasing social and workplace stigma associated with attending work while unwell (Johnson et al., 2021). This shift in norms likely reduced presenteeism even in the absence of PSL mandates. As a result, it is possible that the incremental impact of PSL mandates on working while sick during and after the COVID-19 pandemic may have been attenuated, as even workers without formal PSL coverage may have been more inclined to stay home. Furthermore, downstream outcomes might be more sensitive to day-to-day elements of job quality (e.g., wages, schedule stability) compared to PSL benefits, which are only used occasionally and as necessary when sick. Therefore, while ensuring access to PSL likely contributes positively to public health, its independent, direct effects on worker well-being may be more inherently limited without also addressing more dominant dimensions of job quality (e.g., raising wages, ensuring more stable schedules).

This research is unique in its in-depth analysis of the effects of PSL mandates in the U.S. service sector. Service sector workers arguably stand to benefit significantly from PSL benefits, due to their limited access to fringe benefits, heightened exposure to infectious disease from frequent customer interactions, and limited financial buffer to cope with the consequences of illness without paid leave. More generally, service sector jobs are emblematic of the rise of precarious working conditions in the U.S., from unstable work schedules to a lack of fringe benefits (Schneider and Harknett 2021). The structural nature of this precarity may limit the extent to which employers voluntarily provide benefits like PSL without being mandated to do so, meaning that PSL mandates represent one mechanism for establishing minimum job quality standards in the U.S. service sector. However, it is also important to note that labor protections vary across states, such that two workers at the same firm in different states may differ in their access to paid sick leave. One solution to the patchwork nature of PSL provision is to pass a federal PSL mandate.

Our study has limitations that should be kept in mind. First, data from The Shift Project come from a non-probability sample that uses Facebook as a sampling frame and recruitment platform. Prior work has documented the validity and comparability of the data when benchmarked against probability data sources (Schneider and Harknett, 2022), but our estimates could be biased if some unobserved characteristic affects respondents' propensity to enter our sample and also moderates the relationship between PSL laws and our outcomes. While prior scholarship has assuaged many concerns around the potential bias introduced by unobservables (Schneider and Kristen, 2019, Schneider and Kristen, 2022), we are unable to fully rule out this potential form of bias. Second, while our focus on service sector workers is a key strength of our approach, given the socioeconomic disparities in access to PSL and the heightened risk of illness faced by frontline workers, our findings are not generalizable to all U.S. workers. Third, we excluded workers who worked in sub-state locales that previously passed PSL laws because of low sample size in these cities and counties. Future work could incorporate these city- and county-level dynamics. Finally, we estimate that only 62 % of treated workers ultimately had access to PSL, which is lower than one might expect following a PSL mandate, but we are unable to determine whether this is due to respondents’ awareness or understanding of the benefits available to them, employer non-compliance, exemptions for smaller establishments (e.g., franchises), or for some other reason. Additional research is needed to explore the smaller-than-expected impact.

This research has notable implications for public health. We offer evidence that state PSL laws increase PSL coverage among service sector workers and reduce presenteeism, suggesting that PSL laws pay dividends for public health. If more workers have access to PSL and fewer attend work while sick, then they are less likely to spread illnesses to their coworkers and customers. During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, there were positive public health consequences when workers stayed home while sick to reduce the spread of COVID-19. However, because PSL access has historically been stratified by socioeconomic status (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024; Gupta et al., 2018), service sector workers have typically lacked access to PSL, forcing them to choose between staying home while sick and earning money to support themselves and their families. Guaranteeing PSL offers one solution to this dilemma, exemplifying how labor policies can benefit both workers and public health.
